title: The Lucena position
summary: Reach the Lucena position and build the bridge that lets the pawn queen against the rook.
part.ponte.title: Building the bridge
part.ponte.summary: In the Lucena position, the rook goes to the fourth rank, the king steps out in front of the pawn, and the rook blocks the last check: the pawn promotes.
ex.ponteAssessment01: Play White and win. The black rook, on g2, checks your king, and the black king is far from the pawn, on c6.
ex.ponteAssessment01.hint: The king alone cannot escape the checks. Think about how the king and the rook can work together.
ex.ponteAssessment01.solution: 1.Rg4 blocks the check with the rook protected by the king: that is the bridge. If 1...Rxg4, 2.Kxg4, and the pawn promotes. 1.Kf5 also wins, with the same idea: after the check on f2, the rook blocks on f4.
key.lucena: The Lucena position as Alessandro Salvio published it in 1634: the pawn is one step from promoting and the white king stands in front of it. White wins whoever moves: all that is left is to build the bridge.
history: The Lucena position is the most important one in rook endings: with rook and pawn against rook it is the position that wins, and almost every ending of this kind revolves around reaching it or preventing it. The name is a historical mistake: the Spaniard Luis Ramírez de Lucena wrote one of the first printed chess books around 1497, but the position is not in it; it first appears in 1634, in a book by the Italian Alessandro Salvio. The idea of "building a bridge" with the rook, which is the heart of this lesson, got its name from Aron {{Nimzowitsch|aron-nimzowitsch}} in 1925. Grandmasters know it so well that they rarely need to play it out: in 1999, in Sweden, {{Ulf Andersson|ulf-andersson}} exchanged pawns just to reach it, and his opponent resigned before the bridge ever appeared on the board. In 2002, in {{Cannes|cannes}}, {{Veselin Topalov|veselin-topalov}} beat {{Anatoly Karpov|anatoly-karpov}} in a similar position where no bridge was possible, with a trick to hand over the move.
